title: Standard Enthalpies of Formation
trouble: Students subtract in the wrong order, or forget that an element in its standard state, such as O₂(g), has ΔH°f = 0.

blocks.html: Hess's Law works with any set of reactions. One set is chosen as the universal reference: the reactions that form each compound from its elements. With one table of those, you can find $\Delta H$ for thousands of reactions.

The standard enthalpy of formation, $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}$, is $\Delta H$ for making 1 mol of a substance from its elements in their standard states (1 bar, usually 298 K). For an element in its standard state, such as $\mathrm{O_2(g)}$, $\mathrm{C}$(graphite) or $\mathrm{Fe(s)}$, $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f} = 0$. Then $$\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn} = \sum n\,\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{products}) - \sum n\,\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{reactants}).$$

Imagine taking the reaction in two Hess's-law steps through the elements. First break every reactant down into its elements: that is the reverse of forming them, $-\sum n\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{reactants})$. Then build the products from those same elements: $+\sum n\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{products})$. The elements are the common starting line, set at zero. That is why "products minus reactants" works, and why an element in its standard state adds nothing.

blocks.cap: The elements sit at zero. Methane lies 74.6 kJ below them; the combustion products lie 965.1 kJ below. Combustion drops from one to the other: $-965.1 - (-74.6) = -890.5\ \text{kJ}$.

$\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}$ (kJ/mol)
blocks.cap: Standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Appendix G, from the NIST Chemistry WebBook).

blocks.html: Watch the state symbols. $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}$ is $-285.8\ \text{kJ/mol}$ for $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ but $-241.8\ \text{kJ/mol}$ for $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$. The 44.0 kJ difference is the enthalpy of vaporizing a mole of water at 25 °C, so always use the value that matches the state written in the equation.

blocks.title: Decomposing limestone
steps: $\Delta H^\circ = -1028.4 - (-1207.6) = +179.2\ \text{kJ}$: endothermic, which is why lime kilns must be heated strongly.

blocks.title: Working backward to a formation enthalpy
blocks.q: Ethanol burns by $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH(l)} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $\Delta H^\circ = -1366.8\ \text{kJ}$. Find $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}$ of ethanol.

blocks.html: Subtracting in the wrong order (reactants minus products, which flips the sign), or giving $\mathrm{O_2(g)}$ a nonzero value. Check: combustion reactions should come out strongly negative; and any element in its standard state contributes exactly zero, however many moles of it there are.
